blocks.content: The Polluter Pays Principle means that the absolute liability for harm to the environment extends not only to compensate the victims of pollution but also the cost of restoring the environmental degradation.

rows: Lack of scientific certainty should not delay measures to prevent degradation.
Polluter bears cost of environmental restoration and victim compensation.
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987)
Enterprise engaged in dangerous activity is strictly and fully liable without defenses.
State holds natural resources in trust for the public and cannot alienate them privately.

items: Direct Question Alert: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) declared both Precautionary Principle and Polluter Pays Principle as part of Article 21.
Distinction Alert: Absolute Liability (M.C. Mehta case) does NOT allow the exceptions available under Strict Liability (Rylands v. Fletcher).
Case Law Matching: M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath (1997) explicitly incorporated the Public Trust Doctrine into Indian law.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Precautionary Principle mandates that statutory authorities must anticipate, prevent, and attack the causes of environmental degradation.
The Polluter Pays Principle holds that the financial responsibility for preventing or remedying damage lies with the entity causing environmental harm.
In Indian environmental jurisprudence, the Polluter Pays Principle includes liability to pay compensation to victims and the cost of restoring environmental degradation.
The Public Trust Doctrine imposes a legal duty on the State to protect natural resources like rivers, forests, and air for the public rather than permitting private ownership.
The principle of Absolute Liability, established in the Oleum Gas Leak case (1987), allows no exceptions for hazardous or inherently dangerous industries.
